title: Lifting/training with scoliosis
summary: NH, who has had thoracic scoliosis since his teens, explains how lifting with a crooked spine is possible and recommended. He describes how an uneven shoulder line creates loading and muscular imbalances on presses, curls, deadlifts and squats, and how to correct bar path and use unilateral work. Scoliosis can't be fixed visually, only preserved, so keep training and don't obsess over it.
claims: NH has had scoliosis since his teens; one shoulder sits visibly lower than the other
He believes his scoliosis came from carrying his backpack on one shoulder while his spine was still growing; everyone he knew with scoliosis had it on their backpack side
Children and teens should keep proper posture and carry backpacks on both shoulders
Posture can worsen the shape of the spine but cannot fix scoliosis; it is bone, not muscle
Specialist doctors told him scoliosis would cause lifting problems; his family GP told him to keep lifting because strong back and core muscles prevent pain and spinal degeneration
He has never had a spine injury caused by scoliosis, only problems from the imbalances it creates
His advice only covers lateral thoracic scoliosis; lumbar or forward/backward curvatures may be riskier and are outside his experience
With one shoulder lower, the low side goes into deeper flexion and takes more of the bar's weight on presses: a 45/45 load may feel like 55/35
The overloaded lower shoulder grew noticeably bigger and stronger but was also injured repeatedly on bench press
Fix uneven pressing by actively correcting the bar path until the bar stays level; he now benches with a straight bar pain-free
On curls the opposite happens: the arm on the higher shoulder works through a longer range with worse leverage, so his left biceps is bigger but weaker
To fix a lagging side, add unilateral work: start at 3 sets a week, then 6, then 9 if needed, and progress from there
Avoid mixed grip on deadlifts even with scoliosis; use double overhand
On squats the bar sits tilted on a scoliotic back; correct it by squeezing the upper back harder on the side where the bar dips
Injuries propagate: compensating for one injured side (e.g. a knee) overloads the other side, which can then get hurt too
Not training with scoliosis lets it degenerate; muscles around the spine act like a brace
The visual asymmetry of scoliosis can never be fixed; your crooked posture is your proper posture, so stop obsessing in the mirror and just keep lifting
exercises: actively correct bar path so the bar stays level
lower shoulder otherwise takes more load and gets injured
extra upper-back squeeze on the side where the bar tilts
keep the bar level on a crooked spine
